SITETRANSFORMER.voltage_stability_findings:
**ARMI Manufacturing — Site Transformer | Voltage Stability Findings**

The voltage field for August is running at an average of 492.7 volts — that is sitting above the 480-volt nominal line, and at first glance that looks comfortable. The utility is delivering on the high side of tolerance, which provides a small buffer. But the average value is not the story here. The story is the swing range.

Measured across the full 31-day August dataset, the Site Transformer's voltage field ran a live swing range of 16.4 volts — from a measured maximum of 500.6 volts down to a minimum operating floor of 484.2 volts. For a 480-volt system, a 16.4-volt excursion range represents meaningful variability. The system never technically dropped below the 480-volt nominal floor based on the minimum callout value, but the visual trace in the V view tells a more nuanced story. The triangular dip clusters are repeatedly pressing the voltage toward that lower reference band during production peak events. The minimum of 484.2 volts is the charted floor — but the trajectory of those dips is consistently downward during the moments of maximum load stress.

The triangular voltage-drop pattern is clearly present and it is not random. Approximately 20 to 22 distinct triangular dip clusters are visible across the 31-day span, aligned precisely to what appear to be shift-start load surges. The pattern is daily, rhythmic, and production-driven. Weekend intervals show shallower and less frequent dip events, confirming the source is on-site load behavior, not utility-side insturbance.

The coupling between these voltage dips and the reactive demand events is the most important finding. Every time amperage peaks — confirmed in the M view at a maximum of 302.1 amps — the voltage trace compresses in a triangular profile and the power factor orange band visibly narrows and drops. This is a coupled electromagnetic stress event. Reactive demand is pulling voltage down at the precise moments when current is already at its highest. That combination — high current and low voltage simultaneously — is what accelerates insulation aging in motors, stresses variable frequency drives, and shortens the effective life of capacitor banks if any are present on this circuit.

Device health risk rating for this field: **moderate to high**. The field is not in crisis, but it is absorbing these voltage excursions on every production workday. That is a 20-plus stress cycles per month pattern. Over a year, that is 240-plus coupled stress events absorbed by every device on this bus.

---
SITETRANSFORMER.reactive_harmonic_findings:
**ARMI Manufacturing — Site Transformer | Reactive and Harmonic Findings**

The reactive and harmonic picture on this transformer is where the burden profile becomes clearest. The Baseline Target header confirms a reactive average of 29.9 kVAR carrying across the entire month, with a dataset maximum of 56.3 kVAR. That maximum is the sizing anchor — 56.3 kVAR MAX tells you the peak reactive demand this transformer is managing at its worst production moments.

There is a noted discrepancy between the BT header's 56.3 kVAR MAX and the M-view's 36 kVAR MAX reading. That is a 20.3 kVAR variance — approximately 36 percent — which exceeds the flagging threshold. The most probable explanation is that the M-view is capturing a period-average peak within a specific interval, while the BT header is reporting the dataset-wide absolute maximum. The BT value of 56.3 kVAR MAX is the more conservative and correct anchor for equipment sizing purposes, and it is the value I am carrying forward.

The harmonic behavior adds a second layer of stress on top of the reactive burden. The iTHD average across August is 1.6 percent, which on its own is a reasonable baseline for an industrial facility. But the maximum iTHD of 27.0 percent is the number that demands attention. At 27 percent harmonic distortion, the current waveform is significantly non-sinusoidal during those events. Non-linear harmonic currents do not do useful work — they circulate in the transformer and conductors as heat, they can excite resonance in power factor correction capacitors if any are installed, and they add to the transformer's effective thermal loading well beyond what the kilowatt demand curve alone would suggest.

The critical observation is the synchronization of these events. The harmonic concentration spikes in the M-view purple trace cluster during the same shift-start intervals visible in the voltage dip analysis. These are not independent stressors — reactive surge, voltage depression, current peak, and harmonic injection are all occurring simultaneously at shift starts. That is a compound stress event, not a single-variable problem.

The power factor minimum of 54.9 percent is the most striking individual data point in the entire dataset. Even if it is brief — a flash event at a shift-start surge — a power factor of 54.9 percent means the transformer is at that moment delivering approximately 1.8 times the current needed to accomplish the actual work. That excess current is pure thermal burden on conductors, core, and connected equipment.

---

**ARMI Manufacturing — Site Transformer | Operational Stress Interpretation**

Pulling all four views together — Voltage, Baseline Target, Active-Reactive-Harmonic, and MPTS Simulation — what you are seeing at the Site Transformer is a field under compound, recurring, production-synchronized stress. Each individual metric is explainable in isolation. The real concern is their simultaneous occurrence.

Every weekday shift start at this facility generates a cascade: amperage surges toward the 302.1-amp maximum, reactive demand spikes toward 56.3 kVAR, the voltage field compresses in a triangular dip profile, the power factor collapses — occasionally down to 54.9 percent — and harmonic distortion can peak at 27 percent iTHD at the same moment. This is not a transformer that occasionally experiences stress. This is a transformer that experiences a compound stress event at the start of nearly every production shift, approximately 21 to 22 times per month, every month.

The 500 kVA nameplate rating provides headroom — peak demand of 300.4 kilowatts is not overloading the transformer in an absolute sense. But transformer thermal rating is not just about kilowatt load. Reactive current, harmonic current, and the associated core losses all contribute to effective thermal burden. The thermal consequence reading of $8 per period and $97 per year is the estimated financial proxy for that burden — modest in dollar terms, but meaningful as a signal that the transformer is running hotter than its active load alone would justify.

The field operating above its own 256 kVA daily target on 16 to 18 of approximately 22 production days confirms that the facility's electrical appetite regularly exceeds the operating baseline. This is a facility that is genuinely busy — the productive work is real — but the reactive and harmonic overhead it is carrying means the transformer is working harder than the actual production output requires.

The estimated total consequence is $352 per month, or approximately $4,144 per year. In the context of an industrial operation, that annual figure is not an alarm-level number on its own. But it is a continuous drain — and more importantly, it is a proxy for the mechanical and thermal stress that the dollar figures do not fully capture. Motor insulation aging, drive electronics fatigue, and conductor thermal cycling are real costs that accumulate in maintenance budgets and unplanned downtime, not in monthly energy statements.

This field, in its current untuned state, is a candidate for reactive power compensation that would reduce the reactive overhead, stabilize the voltage dip events, and reduce the thermal burden on the transformer. The compound stress pattern is clear. The cost of inaction is not dramatic in any single month — it is a slow, compounding erosion.

SITETRANSFORMER.simulated_mpts_outcome:
**ARMI Manufacturing — Site Transformer | Simulated MPTS Outcome**

The MPTS Simulation view — the S view — projects what this field looks like after reactive power correction is applied. The headline result is power factor corrected to 99.5 percent and held essentially flat across the entire operating range. Pre-correction, power factor averaged 91.5 percent with a minimum of 54.9 percent and periodic surges of reactive demand up to 56.3 kVAR MAX. Post-correction, the simulation shows reactive average dropping from 29.9 kVAR to 10.1 kVAR, and reactive MAX reducing from 56.3 kVAR to 30.1 kVAR.

That reduction in reactive burden has several downstream effects that are worth naming specifically.

First, the current drawn from the transformer decreases. Lower reactive current means the transformer's actual ampere loading drops closer to what the productive work demand alone requires. Conductor heating is proportional to current squared — so even a moderate reduction in reactive current produces a disproportionate reduction in thermal burden.

Second, the voltage stability improves. The triangular voltage dip events that cluster at shift starts are partially driven by reactive demand surging simultaneously with active load. When reactive demand is compensated locally, the voltage no longer has to absorb that reactive pull at the same moment active current is peaking. The dip profile becomes shallower and the voltage swing range narrows.

Third, the thermal burden on the transformer itself decreases. The $8 per period thermal consequence in the baseline reflects the combined effect of reactive and harmonic current on transformer core and winding temperature. MPTS correction addresses the reactive component directly. While harmonic distortion is a separate stressor, reducing reactive burden gives the transformer thermal headroom that translates to longer insulation life and reduced risk of premature failure.

**MPTS Equipment Sizing (planning-level estimate):**
Using the kVAR MAX anchor of 56.3 kVAR from the BT header — 56.3 ÷ 400 = 0.14 — that rounds up to **1 H490 unit** (400 kVAR rated, approximately $200,000 installed at planning-level estimate). The reactive burden on this transformer is well within the capacity of a single H490, with substantial headroom for load growth. Final sizing and investment figures depend on full engineering scope and site conditions — these are planning estimates only.

The simulation confirms that MPTS correction on the Site Transformer would represent a meaningful improvement in field quality — lower reactive draw, more stable voltage, reduced thermal burden, and a power factor held at 99.5 percent regardless of shift-start load surges. The annualized consequence reduction will depend on final engineering scope, but the direction and magnitude of improvement are clearly supported by the simulation data.

**ARMI Manufacturing — Site Transformer | Recommended Engineering Attention Areas**

Given the untuned field status confirmed across all four views, the following engineering attention areas are prioritized for this transformer:

**1. Reactive Power Compensation Assignment**
The 56.3 kVAR MAX reactive burden is the primary correction target. Engineering should confirm the reactive compensation sizing against a full-month CSV dataset to resolve the discrepancy between the BT-header maximum of 56.3 kVAR and the M-view peak of 36 kVAR. Until that reconciliation is complete, the 56.3 kVAR figure should be used as the conservative planning anchor.

**2. Harmonic Assessment and Mitigation Review**
The 27.0 percent iTHD maximum is elevated and warrants a dedicated harmonic survey. If power factor correction capacitors are installed or planned on this bus, harmonic resonance risk must be evaluated before deployment. A harmonic filter or detuned reactor may be warranted depending on the harmonic spectrum profile.

**3. Voltage Swing Monitoring and Shift-Start Profile**
The 16.4-volt live swing range and the clustered triangular dip events at shift starts should be characterized in detail. A time-stamped voltage event log correlated with production shift schedules would confirm whether MPTS correction alone resolves the dip pattern or whether additional load-sequencing or soft-start measures are needed for the highest-amperage loads.

**4. Transformer Thermal Health Baseline**
Given the recurring compound stress events, a thermal imaging inspection of the transformer, main conductors, and terminations is recommended as a baseline health snapshot before any correction equipment is deployed. This establishes a pre-correction benchmark and identifies any existing insulation degradation that should be addressed prior to optimization.

**5. CSV Data Validation**
All numeric findings in this analysis are vision-extracted from image views. A full Mercury CSV dataset for August 2026 should be loaded to validate the BT header values, confirm the kVAR MAX reconciliation, and provide ground-truth anchors for consequence cost calculations before any engineering commitments are made.

SiteTransformer.voltage_stability_findings:
**ARMI Manufacturing — Site Transformer | Voltage Stability Findings**

The voltage field for August is running at an average of 492.7 volts — that is sitting above the 480-volt nominal line, and at first glance that looks comfortable. The utility is delivering on the high side of tolerance, which provides a small buffer. But the average value is not the story here. The story is the swing range.

Measured across the full 31-day August dataset, the Site Transformer's voltage field ran a live swing range of 16.4 volts — from a measured maximum of 500.6 volts down to a minimum operating floor of 484.2 volts. For a 480-volt system, a 16.4-volt excursion range represents meaningful variability. The system never technically dropped below the 480-volt nominal floor based on the minimum callout value, but the visual trace in the V view tells a more nuanced story. The triangular dip clusters are repeatedly pressing the voltage toward that lower reference band during production peak events. The minimum of 484.2 volts is the charted floor — but the trajectory of those dips is consistently downward during the moments of maximum load stress.

The triangular voltage-drop pattern is clearly present and it is not random. Approximately 20 to 22 distinct triangular dip clusters are visible across the 31-day span, aligned precisely to what appear to be shift-start load surges. The pattern is daily, rhythmic, and production-driven. Weekend intervals show shallower and less frequent dip events, confirming the source is on-site load behavior, not utility-side insturbance.

The coupling between these voltage dips and the reactive demand events is the most important finding. Every time amperage peaks — confirmed in the M view at a maximum of 302.1 amps — the voltage trace compresses in a triangular profile and the power factor orange band visibly narrows and drops. This is a coupled electromagnetic stress event. Reactive demand is pulling voltage down at the precise moments when current is already at its highest. That combination — high current and low voltage simultaneously — is what accelerates insulation aging in motors, stresses variable frequency drives, and shortens the effective life of capacitor banks if any are present on this circuit.

Device health risk rating for this field: **moderate to high**. The field is not in crisis, but it is absorbing these voltage excursions on every production workday. That is a 20-plus stress cycles per month pattern. Over a year, that is 240-plus coupled stress events absorbed by every device on this bus.

SiteTransformer.reactive_harmonic_findings:
**ARMI Manufacturing — Site Transformer | Reactive and Harmonic Findings**

The reactive and harmonic picture on this transformer is where the burden profile becomes clearest. The Baseline Target header confirms a reactive average of 29.9 kVAR carrying across the entire month, with a dataset maximum of 56.3 kVAR. That maximum is the sizing anchor — 56.3 kVAR MAX tells you the peak reactive demand this transformer is managing at its worst production moments.

There is a noted discrepancy between the BT header's 56.3 kVAR MAX and the M-view's 36 kVAR MAX reading. That is a 20.3 kVAR variance — approximately 36 percent — which exceeds the flagging threshold. The most probable explanation is that the M-view is capturing a period-average peak within a specific interval, while the BT header is reporting the dataset-wide absolute maximum. The BT value of 56.3 kVAR MAX is the more conservative and correct anchor for equipment sizing purposes, and it is the value I am carrying forward.

The harmonic behavior adds a second layer of stress on top of the reactive burden. The iTHD average across August is 1.6 percent, which on its own is a reasonable baseline for an industrial facility. But the maximum iTHD of 27.0 percent is the number that demands attention. At 27 percent harmonic distortion, the current waveform is significantly non-sinusoidal during those events. Non-linear harmonic currents do not do useful work — they circulate in the transformer and conductors as heat, they can excite resonance in power factor correction capacitors if any are installed, and they add to the transformer's effective thermal loading well beyond what the kilowatt demand curve alone would suggest.

The critical observation is the synchronization of these events. The harmonic concentration spikes in the M-view purple trace cluster during the same shift-start intervals visible in the voltage dip analysis. These are not independent stressors — reactive surge, voltage depression, current peak, and harmonic injection are all occurring simultaneously at shift starts. That is a compound stress event, not a single-variable problem.
